cards.explanation: The answer is footing. David says he has sunk into the miry depths, where there is no footing. That's mud with nothing solid under it, and no way to push off. I know that feeling, friends, because I once lost a whole afternoon stuck in a dough bowl.

The answer is False. David says it twice: those who hate him do it "without cause," and they are his enemies "…for no reason." Trouble like that is hard enough when you've earned it. It's worse when you haven't.
The answer is repay. David says, "Though I did not steal, I must repay." He's making good on something he didn't take, friends. That is not a fun bill to open.

The answer is that they not be ashamed through him. David says, "May those who hope in You not be ashamed through me…" He has just admitted his folly, and now he's thinking about the people who hope in God. I think that's a man who knows his life touches other people.

The answer is zeal for God's house. David says, "…zeal for Your house has consumed me…" His love for God's house burns so hot that it costs him, and he becomes a stranger to his own brothers. That's a lot to carry for loving the right thing.

The answer is True. David says, "…the insults of those who insult You have fallen on me." The insults aimed at God have landed on David. I think that's what can happen when you stand close to something you love.

The answer is False. David says, "I wept and fasted, but it brought me reproach." And when he made sackcloth his clothing, he says he was "…sport to them." He opens his heart, friends, and they treat it like a joke.

The answer is that he prays to the LORD. Right after the mocking, David says, "But my prayer to You, O LORD, is for a time of favor." Look at that little word "But." The song of the drunkards doesn't get the last word.

The answer is God's abundant loving devotion. David prays, "In Your abundant loving devotion, O God, answer me with Your sure salvation." He's leaning on who God is. In verse 16 he says it again: "…Your loving devotion is good…"
The answer is False. David is in distress, and he says, "Answer me quickly!" He doesn't pretend to be calm about it, friends. He tells God plainly that he needs help soon.

The answer is that David asks God to draw near and redeem his soul. He says, "Draw near to my soul and redeem me…" He wants God close, not far off. I think when you're stuck in the deep, close is the whole point.

The answer is no one. David says, "I looked for sympathy, but there was none, for comforters, but I found no one." He looked for comfort and found none. I think that's one of the loneliest lines in the psalm.

The answer is that they persecute the one God struck. David says, "For they persecute the one You struck and recount the pain of those You wounded." His reason is how they treat people who are already hurting. This is a heavy part of the psalm, friends.

The answer is True. Right after those hard words, David says, "But I am in pain and distress; let Your salvation protect me, O God." He goes right back to being honest with God about where he hurts. And he asks for salvation.

The answer is an ox or a bull. David says his praise "…will please the LORD more than an ox, more than a bull with horns and hooves." In verse 30 he says he will praise God's name in song and exalt Him with thanksgiving. I think that tells you a lot about what he treasures.
The answer is False. In verse 33 David says the LORD "…listens to the needy and does not despise His captive people." So the card has it backwards, friends. The LORD does not despise them.
The answer is rebuild. David says, "For God will save Zion and rebuild the cities of Judah…" The psalm that started in the mud ends with rebuilding, friends.
The answer is those who love His name. David says, "…those who love His name will settle in it." It's not about strength or riches, bakers. It's about love for God's name.
